title: Tuberculous Meningitis
subject: Medicine
summary: A severe CNS infection from Mycobacterium tuberculosis that presents with fever, neck stiffness and altered consciousness. Early diagnosis and prompt anti‑TB therapy plus steroids are life‑saving.

sections.p: Tuberculous meningitis (TBM) is inflammation of the meninges caused by M. tuberculosis. Diagnosis relies on clinical suspicion, CSF findings and imaging, often in settings where culture is slow.
b: Fever, neck stiffness, altered sensorium
CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis, low glucose (<40 mg/dL), high protein (>200 mg/dL)
MRI basal meningeal enhancement

t.b: Confirms TBM; positive in ~30% of cases, takes 4–6 weeks
Looks for primary pulmonary TB; normal in 30% of TBM cases
Suggests prior exposure; not diagnostic alone

sections.p: The British Medical Research Council (MRC) scale classifies TBM into three grades based on consciousness and focal signs, guiding urgency of treatment.
b: Grade I – Alert, no focal deficits
Grade II – Lethargic or confused, possible focal signs
Grade III – Comatose or severe focal deficits

t.b: Assesses level of consciousness; <8 indicates Grade III

sections.p: In low‑resource settings, TBM usually follows untreated pulmonary TB or is reactivation in immunosuppressed patients.
b: Primary pulmonary TB with untreated or partially treated disease
HIV infection (especially CD4 <200)
Malnutrition, diabetes, or chronic steroid use

t.b: High viral load increases risk of TBM

sections.p: Symptoms evolve over weeks. Classic triad is fever, neck stiffness and altered consciousness, but early signs may be subtle.
b: Low‑grade fever, headache, malaise
Neck stiffness, Kernig/Brudzinski signs may be weak
Altered sensorium, seizures, cranial nerve palsies

t.b: Detects papilledema indicating raised intracranial pressure

sections.p: Investigation strategy balances speed and resource availability.

t.b: First step; evaluates CSF cell count, glucose, protein, Gram stain, culture, PCR
Rule out mass lesions; MRI shows basal meningeal enhancement
Full blood count, ESR, CRP, HIV test, liver function

sections.p: TBM can rapidly deteriorate; complications include hydrocephalus, infarcts and cranial nerve palsies.
b: Sudden worsening of consciousness
New focal neurological deficit
Seizure activity

sections.p: Immediate empiric anti‑TB therapy plus steroids, with supportive care and monitoring for complications.
b: Start RHZE (isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) within 24h

t.b: Reduce inflammation and cerebral edema; avoid in bacterial meningitis unless proven TB
External ventricular drain or ventriculoperitoneal shunt if imaging shows obstruction

sections.p: Patients need long‑term therapy and monitoring for drug toxicity; contact tracing and TB control reduce recurrence.
b: Continue RHZE for 10 months after initial 2 months of RHZE+HR

t.b: Monitor for hepatotoxicity from anti‑TB drugs

sections.p: Other meningitides and CNS infections share features but differ in CSF profile and response to treatment.
b: Bacterial meningitis – neutrophilic CSF, high glucose
Cryptococcal meningitis – low glucose, high protein, India ink positive
Cerebral malaria – normal CSF, splenomegaly

sections.p: Low CSF glucose can occur in bacterial meningitis; normal CSF glucose may be seen in early TBM.
b: CSF glucose <40 mg/dL is not specific for TBM

t.b: High in TBM but also in viral meningitis

faq.q: Why is a lumbar puncture delayed in some settings?
faq.a: Because of resource limits or fear of herniation in severe cases; however, it remains essential for diagnosis.

faq.q: Can TBM be treated with steroids alone?
faq.a: No, steroids are adjunctive to anti‑TB drugs; they reduce mortality but do not cure the infection.

faq.q: What is the role of PCR in TBM diagnosis?
faq.a: PCR detects MTB DNA quickly, improving early diagnosis when cultures are slow.

What is the next step? — Start anti‑TB therapy immediately; add steroids; obtain imaging if available. 2. A patient with suspected TBM has a normal CSF glucose.
